podcast.title: College and Jobs
podcast.body: Phil studied English literature at Liverpool University. After his studies, he worked as an editor at a publishing house specializing in textbooks and academic works, and he also took on some teaching responsibilities. "same with Phil, big English lit guy at Liverpool University."

podcast.title: Family Background
podcast.body: Phil Selway comes from a family with an academic background. "He comes from a family of academics."

podcast.title: Joining "On a Friday"
podcast.body: Phil Selway was recruited into "On a Friday" from another Abingdon-based group called Jungle Telegraph. His role was to replace the band's "horrible drum machine," Dr. Rhythm. "Phil Selway was drafted in from an Albington group called Jungle Telegraph to replace that horrible drum machine."

podcast.title: Nickname "Mad Dog"
podcast.body: Phil earned the nickname "Mad Dog" because he "used to be prone to big temper tantrums." "And his nickname is Mad Dog because he used to be prone to big temper tantrums."

xref.title: Hiatus for College (1991)
xref.body: In 1991, "On a Friday" entered an extended hiatus as all five members pursued higher education at different universities. Ed O'Brien went to Manchester University, Colin Greenwood studied English literature at Cambridge, Phil Selway also studied English literature at Liverpool University, and Johnny Greenwood enrolled in both music and psychology programs at Oxford. Tom York decided to take a year off before attending university. "In 1997, a 1991 on a Friday went on an extended sort of hiatus."

xref.title: Downsview Park Stage Collapse (June 16, 2012)
xref.body: On Saturday, June 16, 2012, a stage under construction for a Radiohead concert at Downsview Park in Toronto collapsed around 4:00 PM, an hour before the gates were scheduled to open and just before the band's soundcheck. The stage roof fell, crushing Phil Selba's drum tech, Scott Johnson, with a 5,000-pound video monitor, killing him. Three other people were injured, one seriously, and much of the band's lighting and stage gear was destroyed. "On Saturday, June 16, 2012, a stage was almost finished being built at Downsview Park in Toronto ahead of that night's gig, headlined by Radiohead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Creative Block and Internal Disagreement (Kid A era)
xref.body: Facing immense pressure for their fourth album, Tom Yorke suffered from burnout and a creative block, unable to write anything. In a January 1999 meeting in Paris, the band had no clear direction. Ed O'Brien advocated for a return to "three minute guitar charge pop songs," a view supported by management. However, the Greenwood brothers and Phil Selway felt "lost," leading to difficult and haphazard recording sessions. "Tom was so freaked out and so burned out that he couldn't seem to write anything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Discomfort with Okay Computer Fame
xref.body: Following the massive success of "Okay Computer," Radiohead found the "huge crowds and tons of press coverage" to be unsettling. Drummer Phil Selway coined the phrase "don't read your press, weigh it," and Tom Yorke wore a T-shirt saying in French, "don't swallow your press," reflecting their unease. "All of this attention, however, made the band more than a little uneasy, uncomfortable."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Intentional Sonic Reinvention (Kid A)
xref.body: For "Kid A," Radiohead intentionally "burned it all down and they started from scratch," fundamentally changing their sound to an electronic record. This involved minimal guitar use by Ed O'Brien and Jonny Greenwood, Phil Selway acting more as a computer programmer, and Tom Yorke creating vocals via self-written computer programs. They successfully "destroyed themselves and rebuilt the band as something brand new." "they burned it all down and they started from scratch, which is not an easy thing to do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Scott Johnson's Death
xref.body: Scott Johnson, the drum tech for Phil Selway of Radiohead, died on June 16, 2012, during the Downsview Park stage collapse in Toronto. He had been with the band for approximately two years. Johnson was crushed by a video monitor weighing almost 2,300 kilograms, with the official cause of death reported as "crushing injury of head and brain." "Scott Johnson, Phil Selway's drum tech, who had been with the band for about two years, was crushed by a video monitor that weighed almost 2,300 kilograms."
